925.title: The great Buddha of Nara
925.hook: an emperor asks everyone, down to a handful of earth, to help cast a giant bronze Buddha
925.howItsDone: Todaiji in Nara is still a working temple of the Kegon school, where pilgrims and visitors come to bow before the great Buddha, and monks hold regular services in the hall.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Japan: a gilt bronze Buddha from Korea, a divided court, and Prince Shotoku. Your line was the teaching arrives. What new thing did you give a fair hearing? Day nine hundred twenty-five.

The doors of the hall swing open, and at first the eyes don't know what they're looking at. A bronze knee, higher than your head. A hand raised, palm out, bigger than a person. Far above, in the dim light, a calm face looking down over everyone who walks in. Schoolchildren crane their necks. Deer wander outside the gate. This is Todaiji, in Nara, and the seated figure inside is the great Buddha. Today, Vairocana, and the strange invitation that made it.
screen: `A KNEE HIGHER THAN YOUR HEAD.` → `A CALM FACE FAR ABOVE.` → `TODAIJI, IN NARA.`

segments.voice: First, the invitation. Japan's official chronicle, the Shoku Nihongi, preserves Emperor Shomu's edict calling for the image. He says he has the wealth and the power of the land, and could simply order it made. But that, he says, would miss the point. So he asks that anyone who wishes to help, even by bringing a single branch of grass or a handful of earth, be allowed to share in the work. A giant made of countless small offerings. Second, which Buddha. The great Buddha is Vairocana, called Rushana in Japanese, the Buddha at the center of the Flower Garland Sutra. That's the same sutra behind the Huayan school, the one Uisang carried home to Korea. In Japan it's called Kegon, and Todaiji became its great temple. In that sutra, Vairocana's light reaches into every world. A Buddha that large is trying to show something that large. Third, the opening of the eyes. When the image was finished, a ceremony was held to open its eyes, with an Indian monk, Bodhisena, holding the brush. Cords tied to the brush ran out into the crowd, so that many hands could hold them and share in the moment. Fourth, the face. Fire and war have damaged the image more than once, and the head you see today is a later recasting, not the first one. Through every repair, the expression stayed the same kind: not triumphant, calm. Vast things can be frightening: the sea at night, the sky over a desert. Here, vastness is shown at peace, a hand raised as if to say, don't be afraid.
screen: `A HANDFUL OF EARTH.` · `VAIROCANA OF THE FLOWER GARLAND.` · `CORDS TO THE BRUSH.` · `VASTNESS AT PEACE.` · then, large: `VAST AND CALM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture something vast. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind the biggest thing you've ever stood in front of: an ocean, a mountain, a night sky, a cathedral ceiling, a canyon. Let it fill your inner sight. Notice the body's first response, a tightening or a widening. Then see if you can let it be calm, the way the bronze face is calm. Big, and at rest. Breathe inside that size for the rest of the time. The bell holds the time.
Vairocana. The great Buddha of Nara, cast in bronze at Todaiji with the help of anyone who brought a handful of earth, vast and at peace. Today's word.
Your line: vast and calm. Today, look up at the sky once, on purpose, for one full breath, and let something that big be calm. Day nine hundred twenty-five.

926.title: Mount Hiei
926.hook: Saicho founds Tendai on Mount Hiei, the mountain where later founders trained
926.howItsDone: Mount Hiei is still the head center of the Tendai school, where monks train in study, meditation and ritual, and Saicho is honored by Tendai Buddhists as Dengyo Daishi.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vairocana, the great Buddha of Nara, made with anyone's handful of earth. Your line was vast and calm. When you looked up at the sky, what did you notice? Day nine hundred twenty-six.

A young monk, newly ordained, leaves the great temples of Nara behind and climbs a forested mountain to the northeast of where Kyoto now stands. He builds a small hall and sits in it. He isn't trying to start anything grand. He wants quiet, and the sutras, and time. But the hut on the mountain grows. Students come, then more halls, then a whole monastic world among the cedars. Generations later, monks who trained on that slope will come down and start schools of their own. The young monk's name is Saicho. Today, Mount Hiei.
screen: `A YOUNG MONK CLIMBS.` → `A SMALL HALL AMONG CEDARS.` → `THE HUT GROWS.`

segments.voice: First, the school. Saicho traveled to China and studied the Tiantai teaching, one of the Chinese schools we met earlier, built around the Lotus Sutra. Back in Japan he founded it on Mount Hiei, where it took the name Tendai. Tendai held a wide range under one roof: study of the Lotus Sutra, meditation, the monastic precepts and esoteric ritual. Second, the training. Saicho wrote rules for the students of his mountain school, and they are demanding. He asks students to stay on the mountain for twelve years, without going down, studying and practicing the whole time. In the same writings he says that a person who lights up one corner of the world is a treasure of the nation. Not a famous person. Not a powerful one. Someone who brightens the corner they're standing in. Third, the long reach. Tradition remembers several later founders of Japanese schools as having trained on Mount Hiei before they went their own way: Honen and Shinran, who taught the Pure Land path; Dogen, who brought a Zen lineage home from China; Nichiren, who centered everything on the Lotus Sutra. They taught very differently, and their schools have their own stories, which this path will reach. But they learned their first lessons on the same slope. And one more face from a few days back: Ennin, who watched the persecution of 845 with his diary in hand, was Saicho's student, and returned to lead the mountain. Fourth, the training ground. There may be a slope like this in your own story: a kitchen, a workshop, a classroom, a team, where you learned the basics before going your own way.
screen: `SAICHO BRINGS TIANTAI HOME.` · `TWELVE YEARS ON THE MOUNTAIN.` · `FOUNDERS WHO TRAINED THERE.` · `A SLOPE IN YOUR OWN STORY.` · then, large: `THE MOUNTAIN SCHOOL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor your training ground. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the place where you first learned something that still shapes you: a family table, a gym, a church hall or temple, a first job, a library. See it as clearly as you can, the light, the smell, the people. Remember one teacher there, named or unnamed. If you'd like, thank that place silently, in a few plain words. The bell holds the time.
Mount Hiei. The mountain where Saicho founded Tendai, wrote his rules for long training, and where later founders of Japanese schools first learned. Today's word.
Your line: the mountain school. Today, light up one corner: one desk, one room, one conversation, and leave it a little brighter than you found it. Day nine hundred twenty-six.

927.title: Koyasan
927.hook: Kukai founds Shingon on Mount Koya; pilgrims still walk his island route
927.howItsDone: Pilgrims walk the Shikoku temple circuit associated with Kukai, often dressed in white with a staff and a sedge hat, and some also climb to Koyasan to pay respects at his mausoleum.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mount Hiei, where Saicho built the Tendai school and later founders trained. Your line was the mountain school. Which place taught you the most? Day nine hundred twenty-seven.

On the island of Shikoku, a walker in white sets off down a country road with a wooden staff and a wide sedge hat. There's no one else in sight. Still, pilgrims on this road have a phrase for it: two traveling together. One is the walker. The other, they say, is Kukai, the monk whose memory this long loop of temples carries. The staff, in their telling, stands for him. So the walker is never quite alone. Today, we follow that companion back to the mountain where his school made its home. Koyasan.
screen: `A WALKER IN WHITE.` → `TWO TRAVELING TOGETHER.` → `BACK TO THE MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: Kukai was a Japanese monk who, his biographies say, sailed to China to study and came home with an esoteric teaching that works through body, speech and mind at once. Hands shaped into gestures. Sacred sounds chanted. The mind resting on a figure of the Buddha. His school took the name Shingon, true word, after the mantras at its heart. He taught at court in the capital, where a great temple was later put in his care. But he also wanted a place apart, far from politics, for meditation. So Kukai asked the emperor for a mountain, a high valley ringed by peaks, and on Mount Koya he began a monastery. Koyasan. Over time it grew into a town of temples, with halls, monks, and a forest of graves under old cedars. And here the history turns into faith. Kukai came to be honored by the title Kobo Daishi. Tradition says he did not die on the mountain but entered deep meditation, and that he is still sitting there in the inner sanctuary. Monks, tradition says, still bring meals to his hall. Shingon followers hold this in different ways: some take it plainly, some as a way of saying his teaching is alive. Either way, the road matters. Pilgrims walk the temple loop on Shikoku, his home island, on foot, by bus, or a section at a time, and some finish by climbing to Koyasan to give thanks. The pilgrim isn't discovering anything new. The temples are known. The road itself is the practice. One step, one temple, one bow, and, in the pilgrims' telling, the companion walking beside them is the one they came to meet.
screen: `KUKAI BRINGS HOME A TRUE WORD.` · `A MOUNTAIN, FAR FROM COURT.` · `TRADITION SAYS HE IS STILL SITTING.` · `THE ROAD ITSELF IS THE PRACTICE.` · then, large: `THE PILGRIM'S ROAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk a small pilgrimage. If you can stand, choose a short route: to a window, a doorway, a plant, and back. Walk it slowly. At the far end, pause and lower your head, or simply stop for one breath. If you can't walk right now, trace the route with your eyes instead. Then sit, and let the walk keep going inside: one step, one breath. If you'd like a companion, picture someone walking beside you. The bell holds the time.
Koyasan. Mount Koya, where Kukai made a home for his Shingon school, and where, tradition says, he still sits in meditation. Today's word.
Your line: the pilgrim's road. Today, turn one ordinary walk, to the bus or to the kitchen, into a small pilgrimage, with one pause at the end. Day nine hundred twenty-seven.

928.title: New schools
928.hook: in the Kamakura era, Pure Land, Zen and Nichiren teachers found new schools for ordinary people
928.howItsDone: Japanese Pure Land Buddhists recite Namu Amida Butsu, Zen practitioners sit zazen, and Nichiren Buddhists chant Namu Myoho Renge Kyo, often together at temples or in home groups.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Koyasan, where Kukai made his mountain home and pilgrims still walk his road. Your line was the pilgrim's road. Which ordinary walk became a small pilgrimage? Day nine hundred twenty-eight.

Mount Hiei trained monk after monk in long years of study. Some of them came down the mountain with a blunt question: what about everyone who can't live up here? The farmer. The fisherman. The mother with a baby on her back. The soldier who may not see next spring. Can they walk this path too, today, without years in a monastery? In the Kamakura era, several teachers answered yes, each in a different way, and each answer became a school. Today's word: new schools.
screen: `DOWN FROM THE MOUNTAIN.` → `WHAT ABOUT EVERYONE ELSE?` → `SEVERAL ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: Three doors opened. The first is Pure Land. Honen taught that in a hard age, the way open to anyone is to call on Amida Buddha by name, with trust: Namu Amida Butsu. His student Shinran went further: even the calling, he taught, is Amida's gift, not your own achievement. The second door is Zen. Eisai brought Rinzai Zen back from China, with its sharp questions, and Dogen brought Soto Zen, teaching that sitting itself, just sitting, is already awakening at work. No ladder to climb first. The third door is Nichiren. He taught that the Lotus Sutra holds the whole teaching, and that chanting its title, Namu Myoho Renge Kyo, opens it to anyone. Here's what the three share, even where they argue. Each puts one practice at the heart of the path: a name, a sitting, a title. You don't need a library. You need a voice, or a cushion, or a breath. And these founders, their biographies say, had studied on Mount Hiei first, then left to teach what had opened the way for them. The schools disagreed with each other, sometimes sharply, about faith and effort and which teaching stands at the center, and their heirs still discuss it. They also reached different people: Pure Land and Nichiren preachers went out to villages and towns, while Zen found early patrons among warriors and the court. That's the honest picture: several new schools, each in its own way carrying the path beyond the monastery walls.
screen: `PURE LAND: CALL THE NAME.` · `ZEN: JUST SIT.` · `NICHIREN: CHANT THE TITLE.` · `ONE PRACTICE, WITHIN REACH.` · then, large: `FOR ORDINARY PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one new beginning. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing in your life that started fresh: a move, a job, a friendship, a habit, a morning you decided to live differently. Name it quietly. Notice what you had to leave behind to begin it, the way these teachers left the mountain. Then let the name go and rest with the breath. Each breath is a small new beginning of its own. The bell holds the time.
New schools. Pure Land, Zen and Nichiren teachers in the Kamakura era, each putting one practice within reach of ordinary people. Today's word.
Your line: for ordinary people. Today, make one good thing easier for someone else to start: share a first step, lend a tool, or explain it plainly. Day nine hundred twenty-eight.

929.title: Zen and the arts
929.hook: tea, gardens, ink painting and poetry shaped by practice
929.howItsDone: Zen temples in Japan keep tea gatherings, dry gardens and brush calligraphy as part of temple life, and lay students learn the tea way, ink painting and flower arranging as disciplines of attention.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the new schools: a name, a sitting, a title, each within reach. Your line was for ordinary people. What did you make easier for someone? Day nine hundred twenty-nine.

A bowl of green tea, turned once before it's handed over. A garden with no water in it, only raked gravel and a few stones. A circle drawn in black ink with one stroke. A short poem about an old pond and a frog jumping in. None of these look like religion. No altar, no sermon, no scripture read aloud. And yet in Japan, people have tied each of them to Zen practice, to monks and to the people who sat with them. Today: how sitting still spilled out into the hands. Wabi.
screen: `TEA, STONE, INK, A POEM.` → `NO ALTAR, NO SERMON.` → `SITTING SPILLS INTO THE HANDS.`

segments.voice: The idea underneath is simple. If awakening isn't somewhere else, it can show up in anything done fully. Take tea. In the tea way, every move is set: how you fold the cloth, how you whisk, how you turn the bowl before you offer it. The rules aren't fussy for their own sake. They clear the room, so attention has nothing left to do but be here. A saying in the tea world puts it plainly: tea and Zen, one taste. Then the dry garden. Raked gravel can be read as water, stones as islands or mountains, and some of these gardens are made to be sat beside rather than walked through. The raking itself is practice, done again tomorrow and the day after. Then ink. Zen teachers have painted the enso, a circle made in a single movement of the brush. You can't go back and fix it. The circle shows the state of the hand that made it, wobble and all. And the short poem catches one moment so plainly it hardly seems to have an author. Across all of these, two threads run. Simplicity: take away until what's left is enough. And presence: the thing is done now, once, with the whole person. Japanese has a word for the beauty of what's plain, worn and imperfect: wabi. A cracked tea bowl, carefully mended, can be prized above a flawless one. Not every artist was a monk, and not every cup of tea is Zen. But the arts gave practice somewhere to live outside the meditation hall.
screen: `ANYTHING DONE FULLY.` · `TEA: EVERY MOVE IS SET.` · `A CIRCLE IN ONE STROKE.` · `TAKE AWAY UNTIL IT'S ENOUGH.` · then, large: `PRACTICE IN THE ARTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make one thing simply. Choose something small you can do right where you are: pour a glass of water, fold a napkin, or draw one circle on a scrap of paper. Do it once, slowly, with your whole attention, and don't fix it afterward. Look at what you made. Then sit, and let your hands rest open in your lap. If your mind wants to redo it, notice that, and come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
Wabi. The Japanese word for the beauty of what's plain, worn and imperfect, found in tea, gardens, ink and poems shaped by Zen practice. Today's word.
Your line: practice in the arts. Today, do one everyday task the way a tea master would, slowly and simply, from start to finish. Day nine hundred twenty-nine.

930.title: Tibet's first king
930.hook: Songtsen Gampo and his two Buddhist queens, from Nepal and China
930.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists visit the Jokhang in Lhasa to honor the Jowo statue, walking around the temple and making full-length prostrations, and they remember Songtsen Gampo and his queens in histories and festivals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, wabi, Zen and the arts: tea, raked gravel, one circle of ink. Your line was practice in the arts. What did you do simply, start to finish? Today the road turns to Tibet. Day nine hundred thirty.

High on the plateau, a king is building an empire. Songtsen Gampo, the Tibetan histories say, ruled Tibet and pushed its borders outward. He made alliances by marriage, taking wives from powerful neighbors. Two of them came over the mountains: a princess from Nepal and a princess from China. Each one, the story goes, brought something with her that would outlast the empire. Not gold. Not soldiers. An image of the Buddha. Today: Songtsen Gampo.
screen: `A KING ON THE PLATEAU.` → `A PRINCESS FROM NEPAL, ONE FROM CHINA.` → `EACH BRINGS A BUDDHA.`

segments.voice: Tibetan histories give the queens names. From Nepal came Bhrikuti. From China came Wencheng. Each, tradition says, carried a sacred image of the Buddha, and temples were raised in Lhasa to house them. One of those images, the statue called the Jowo, is linked by tradition to Wencheng, and it is honored in the Jokhang temple in Lhasa today. Pilgrims walk around the temple and stretch out full length on the stones in front of it. The same histories credit the king's reign with another gift. A minister, tradition says, was sent to India and came back with a way to write Tibetan, so that one day the teachings could be translated. Later Tibetans remember Songtsen Gampo as the first of the dharma kings, the kings who welcomed the teaching, and they tell his story in sacred terms: the king as a form of Chenrezig, the bodhisattva of compassion, and the two queens as forms of Tara. Historians read these accounts carefully. They come from later Tibetan histories, and how much the king practiced himself is debated. But notice what the story chooses to remember. Not the battles. The arrivals. Two women who left home, crossed the mountains, and carried something precious into a land that didn't yet have it. The teaching came in with them quietly, as a gift in a bride's baggage.
screen: `TWO QUEENS, TWO BUDDHAS.` · `THE JOWO IN THE JOKHANG.` · `A WAY TO WRITE TIBETAN.` · `THE STORY REMEMBERS THE ARRIVALS.` · then, large: `TWO QUEENS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor someone who brought a gift. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a person who carried something good into your life from somewhere else: a recipe, a song, a book, a way of praying, a way of being kind. Picture the road they traveled to reach you. If you pray, you can give thanks for them. If not, simply hold their face in mind with gratitude, and let the breath carry it. The bell holds the time.
Songtsen Gampo. Remembered by Tibetans as the first of the dharma kings, whose two queens, tradition says, each brought a Buddha. Today's word.
Your line: two queens. Today, thank one person, out loud or in a message, for something good they brought into your life. Day nine hundred thirty.

931.title: The abbot is invited
931.hook: King Trisong Detsen invites the Indian abbot Shantarakshita
931.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists honor Shantarakshita, Padmasambhava and King Trisong Detsen together as founders of the teaching in Tibet, and it is customary for students to formally request teachings before a teacher gives them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Songtsen Gampo, Tibet's first king, and the two queens who, tradition says, each brought a Buddha. Your line was two queens. Whom did you thank? Day nine hundred thirty-one.

A king can build a temple. He can't build a teacher. Later in Tibet's story, another king, Trisong Detsen, wanted the Buddha's teaching to take real root in his land: not only images in temples, but monks, study and practice. For that he needed someone who knew it from the inside. So he did what a king can do: he sent an invitation, over the Himalaya, to India. Today: Shantarakshita.
screen: `A KING CAN'T BUILD A TEACHER.` → `ROOTS, NOT ONLY IMAGES.` → `AN INVITATION TO INDIA.`

segments.voice: The man invited was Shantarakshita, a learned Indian abbot and a philosopher in his own right. Tibetans remember him as the great abbot. He came. He taught the foundations: avoid harm, do good, see how actions bring their results. Then trouble came too. The Tibetan accounts tell of floods, lightning and sickness, and of people who said the old gods of the land were angry at the newcomer. Some at court opposed the new teaching outright. And here the abbot did something worth noticing. He didn't insist he was enough. Tradition says he told the king that this work needed a different kind of teacher, one who could meet those forces head on, and he named him. The abbot stepped back to make room. Notice how many invitations are in this stretch of the story. A queen comes from Nepal and a queen from China. A king invites an abbot. The abbot asks the king to invite someone else. The teaching doesn't march in. It is asked in, and then it asks for help. And that's this whole week, too. We began at the great Buddha of Nara, climbed Mount Hiei and Mount Koya, watched new schools open for ordinary people and practice spill into tea and ink, then crossed to Tibet, where two queens carried the Buddha in. Again and again in this stretch, someone asks, or is asked. Tomorrow, we meet the one the abbot named.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: invite someone wise. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one question you've been carrying alone. Then think of one person who might know more about it than you do: a teacher, an elder, a friend who's been through it. Picture asking them. Notice whatever makes asking hard, and let it sit beside you without obeying it. If you pray, you can ask for help in finding the right person. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
